exclude_reason: Horizon is week-ahead, not day-ahead: H = 168 hourly steps from a 336-hour look-back, and the paper positions itself explicitly against day-ahead work — "Although day-ahead forecasting has been widely studied in the NEM, week-ahead hourly forecasting remains relatively underexplored despite its practical importance" (Sec. I, p.1). It IS genuine electricity PRICE forecasting (RRP) with weather-derived inputs (temperature, wind speed, humidity, cloud cover) plus AEMO renewable generation forecasts, so it fails only the horizon criterion. Compounding this, the Australian NEM is a real-time dispatch market settled at five-minute resolution with rebidding, so there is no day-ahead auction and no day-ahead bidding gate against which input admissibility could be assessed. Columns are coded anyway as a near-miss/borderline record: the paper is a clean instance of the availability-timing gap, naming weather variables and renewable "forecasts" while never stating their vintage, publication time, or availability at the forecast origin.

evidence_quotes: Sec. III-A Dataset Description, p.3: "The dataset is obtained from the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) [22] and World Weather Online [23], covering the period from April 2024 to March 2025 with diverse seasonal and volatility regimes. It includes electricity price (RRP), total demand, net interchange, renewable generation forecasts (solar and wind), and weather-related variables such as temperature, wind speed, humidity, and cloud cover." [Supports input_type and weather_source: the renewable inputs are explicitly labelled 'forecasts' but no product, horizon or issue time is named, while the four weather variables are never characterised as observations or as forecasts. Ref. [23] is only 'World Weather Online, "Weather api," https://www.worldweatheronline.com/weather-api/, accessed: 2026-04-09' - an access date, not a data vintage.] || Sec. II-A Problem Formulation, pp.2-3: "Let y_t denote the electricity price at time t, and let z_t represent the corresponding exogenous variables, including demand, renewable generation, and weather features. Given a historical input window of length L, the model input is defined as: x_t = {y_{t-L+1:t}, z_{t-L+1:t}}" ... "where L = 336 represents a two-week look-back window and H = 168 corresponds to the week-ahead forecasting horizon." [Supports input_type: the formal input set contains exogenous values only up to the forecast origin t, i.e. past-only, which is directly contradicted by the limitations paragraph quoted below. The paper never resolves which convention was actually implemented.] || Sec. IV-A Implications, Limitations and Future Work, p.6: "The study assumes the availability of accurate exogenous variables such as demand and weather data. In practice, these inputs are forecasted and may introduce additional uncertainty." [Supports publication_time_stated and gate_admissibility_checked: this is the paper's only engagement with availability timing. It is an admitted assumption rather than a check, and it implies realised/actual exogenous values were used as stand-ins for what would operationally be forecasts - the opposite of verifying admissibility. No publication or dissemination time is given for any input.] || Sec. III-B Experimental Setup, p.4: "An expanding window evaluation strategy is adopted, with four consecutive weekly test sets from March 1 to March 28, 2025. For each test week, models are trained using all historical data available from April 2024 up to the forecast period, ensuring a strict temporal separation between training and evaluation." [Supports gate_admissibility_checked: the only temporal-integrity claim in the paper concerns the training/evaluation split, not the availability of exogenous inputs at the forecast origin. 'Strict temporal separation' is asserted for the estimation sample alone; nothing verifies that the weather and renewable-forecast values fed into each 168-hour forecast were published before that forecast was made.]
